title: What to have ready before kickoff
metaTitle: What to have ready before kickoff
excerpt: Before kickoff, gather the accounts, a rough offer, access to the current site, and the name of the person who can approve. Missing access spends the first week on waiting.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall. The string is the path you can draw once access, the offer, and an approver are already in the room.
caption: Kickoff goes faster when the path is already pinned. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which accounts should be ready before kickoff?
faqs.answer: Have the domain registrar, the current host, analytics, and any store or content admin you expect the project to touch, on company-owned logins rather than a personal account you might lose. If a payment provider or email tool is in scope, have that admin too. You can invite the studio during kickoff, and you cannot invite them to a login nobody can find.

faqs.question: How polished does the offer need to be?
faqs.answer: A rough offer is enough: who it is for, what you do, and the one action the site should earn. Three references you like, and a note on what must not change, are more useful than a finished slogan. The project can rewrite the sentence. It cannot invent the business.

faqs.question: Who needs to be at kickoff?
faqs.answer: The person who can approve the work, plus anyone who holds access the project will stall without. A large audience of stakeholders turns kickoff into a replay. People who need to be informed can read the note afterward. The approver has to be able to say yes in the room.

markdown:
A website project kickoff goes faster when four things are already true: the accounts exist, the offer can be said in a few sentences, someone can open the current site, and one person is named who can approve. Missing access is what burns the first week.

Kickoff is not the moment to discover the domain is in a former freelancer’s email. It is the moment the schedule starts. Everything you can find before that hour is a day you do not spend searching.

## Accounts the company owns

List the logins the project might touch, and make sure the company owns them.

- The domain registrar, and the person who can change DNS.
- The host or the place the current site deploys.
- Analytics, if you have it, including who can add a teammate.
- The content admin, the store admin, or both.
- Email for the domain, if the launch will send from it.
- A payment provider, if you take orders.

Use shared or role-based access where you can. A single password in one person’s head is how vacations become outages. You do not need to hand over ownership on day one. You do need a path to invite the studio, and a path to remove them later. The repository, when it exists, should be in your organization.

If an account is missing, say so before kickoff. “We think the domain is at this registrar, and we are recovering the login” is a real status. Pretending it is handled means the launch week plan is fiction. Recovery can take days. Start it when you sign, not when someone asks for the DNS panel.

Brand files belong on this list too. Logos, type, and any colors you have already committed to. If they live in an old thread, collect them into one folder. Hanabi’s portal is where those files, the docs, and later project updates can live after delivery. Before kickoff, a single folder is enough. The point is that the studio is not redrawing a logo you already approved because nobody could find the file.

## A rough offer

Write a short brief. Who the site or product is for. The one action it should earn. Three references you like, and why. What must not change: a name, a URL, a promise you have already made to customers.

This can be half a page. A forty-page deck usually repeats a strategy the page cannot hold. The studio needs the constraint, not the archive of every meeting that led to it.

Google’s notes on [helpful, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) are a good mirror for the brief. The future page should be useful to the person it is for, and it should come from real knowledge of the offer. If your brief cannot say who that person is, kickoff will spend itself on that question. Answer a working version now. You are allowed to revise it when you see the page. You are not helped by arriving with “everyone” as the audience.

Bring facts you will stand behind. Prices, if they are public. A list of products you still sell. The names of customers you are willing to show, if proof is part of the site. Inventing these during design produces pretty pages full of placeholders, and placeholders hide layout problems until the real words arrive.

If you have nothing public yet, bring the sentence you would say in a room. The project can shape it. It should not be the first time you have tried to say it.

## Access to the current site

If a site, a shop, or a product already exists, the studio needs to see it the way a maintainer sees it, not only as a visitor.

For a marketing site, that means the repo or the CMS, and a note on how a page gets published. For a shop, it means the catalog admin and a sample order path. For a product, it means a staging login and the workflow you care about. Screenshots are a start. They go stale, and they hide the editing path that may be the reason you are rebuilding.

Export what a migration must not lose, or know who can. Product URLs, titles, and the customer and order records you are allowed to keep. A WooCommerce shop, for example, should not reach kickoff with nobody able to export the catalog. The first week then becomes archaeology.

Read-only access is enough at the start. Production credentials can wait until a named person needs them. Write down which environments exist: live, staging, and the one nobody should touch. A kickoff that puts a stranger in production “to look around” is how accidents happen.

If there is no current site, say that. The access task becomes the accounts you will create: the domain, the repo, the analytics property, the place content will live. Creating them in your name, during the first days, is part of owning the result.

## The person who can approve

Name one approver. They can take advice. They cannot be a committee that only meets on Thursdays if the review is on Wednesday.

The approver should be at kickoff. If they cannot attend, move kickoff. A session that “gathers input” and then waits a week for a yes has not kicked off. It has interviewed.

Tell the approver what they will be asked to accept: the slice, the references, the date, and the rule for changes. They do not need to design. They need to decide. Feedback like “clearer” or “more serious” is usable. A competing redesign in the margin, from someone who is not the approver, can be heard and parked.

Also name a backup for access, not for taste. If the approver is traveling, someone else should still be able to unlock the registrar. Taste can wait a day. A locked domain cannot.

Write the name in the kickoff note. “Alex approves. Jordan can grant access.” Future you, and the studio, will use that line when a stakeholder appears with a new homepage in week four.

## What can wait

Do not block kickoff on perfection.

Final photography can wait if you have enough real images to design the crop, or a clear plan to shoot. A finished brand book can wait if the logo files and a sentence of voice are real. Legal pages can wait if you know who will write them and when. A complete sitemap of every future idea can wait. The slice cannot.

Have the schedule constraints that are real: a ship date, an event, a season. Have the constraints that are not: “we would like it soon” can be translated into a date or dropped.

A good kickoff ends with the slice, the channel you will use, the approver, and the access still missing, each with an owner. If you leave with a mood and a shared folder of inspiration, you have not started. You have decorated the delay.

The brief itself has a tighter form when the project is a marketing site. That checklist lives in [how to brief a studio for a marketing site](/blog/brief-a-studio-for-a-marketing-site).

When the four things in this piece are in hand, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) if you have not already, or bring them to kickoff if the project is agreed. The hour should spend itself on the work, not on finding the password.
